newsitem.title: KENYA: Amnesty says most Rwanda genocide trials unfair.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty says most Rwanda genocide trials unfair.

text.p: Most trials in Rwanda for genocide and crimes against humanity are unfair with defendants presumed guilty unless proved innocent, Amnesty International said on Tuesday.
The London-based human rights group said observations of trials in January and February and a review of the genocide law had revealed serious problems since trials began in December.
"In the climate of bitterness and suspicion which prevails after the genocide, many defendants accused of genocide are considered guilty unless proved innocent," it said in a report.

"That trials are being held at all represents a significant step towards restoring justice in Rwanda, but serious flaws in both law and practice put at risk the lives of those charged and the attempts at rebuilding Rwanda's justice system," it added.
"For the government's efforts and the trials themselves to be effective, they need to conform to international standards".
At least 18 people have been sentenced to death in Rwanda for involvement in the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
Amnesty said some trials only lasted for a few hours.

It said Rwanda's Code of Criminal Procedure gave the defence only eight days to prepare for a trial and it was hard for defendants to prepare because of overcrowded prisons, an absence of writing materials and a lack of aid for the illiterate.
The Amnesty report said most prosecutors and judges received only up to six months training and had no prior legal training.
It said using judicial officials with inadequate training seriously jeopardised the outcome and the conduct of trials.
It said in 1995 and 1996 a number of judicial officials had been removed from their posts, apparently because of government or military interference, which had continued this year.
Celestin Kayibanda, the prosecutor in the southern city of Butare, was arrested in May 1996 and charged with genocide apparently because he had denounced official interference in the judiciary.
Amnesty said in at least two trials in Rwanda courts had done nothing to prevent defendants being jeered by spectators.

"Public statements by government officials declaring all defendants guilty in the months preceding the trials add to the risk of erroneous convictions and put judges under real or perceived pressure," it said.
It said judges failed to investigate defendants who said they incriminated themselves under torture and the government should direct officials to exclude any confession obtained by torture.
It said trials showed a serious disregard for international conventions and there were only 16 defence lawyers in Rwanda for about 100,000 prisoners awaiting trial on charges of genocide.
Amnesty said many lawyers were reluctant to become involved due to a climate of hostility towards those accused of genocide.
"The establishment of an adequately trained, permanent body of Rwandese defence lawyers is essential for the many trials which will be taking place in the months and years ahead."
It said defendants sentenced to death had failed appeals but by the start of this month their appeals had not yet been heard.
